title: The Book of Ecclesiastes
lead: Ecclesiastes, the book of Qohelet, the teacher who speaks as a king in Jerusalem and finds that everything under the sun is vapor: who wrote it and when, how its frame narrator and its contradictions shape it, why the rabbis debated its place in Scripture, and how Jews and Christians have read it.

sections.h: Qohelet and Israel's other wisdom books
sections.b: Ecclesiastes belongs with Proverbs and Job among the Bible's wisdom books. Proverbs teaches that the wise and the righteous will flourish (Proverbs 3:1–2; Proverbs 10:27); Job and Ecclesiastes test that teaching against what people actually see. Job argues with God over one man's suffering; Qohelet looks at the whole world and finds that the same death comes to the wise and the fool (Ecclesiastes 2:14–16) and that the race is not always to the swift (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Yet he still holds that wisdom is better than folly (Ecclesiastes 2:13) and quotes many sayings like those of Proverbs (Ecclesiastes 7:1–14; Ecclesiastes 10). Later Jewish wisdom continues the conversation: Sirach, written in Hebrew about 180 BC, and the Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, which seems to answer readers who drew pleasure-seeking conclusions from Qohelet's words (Wisdom of Solomon 2:1–9).

sections.b: The New Testament never quotes Ecclesiastes directly, but several passages echo it. Paul's words that the creation was "made subject to emptiness" (Romans 8:20) use the Greek word mataiotes, the same word the Greek Ecclesiastes uses for hevel. Jesus' parable of the rich fool, who plans to eat, drink and be merry and dies that night (Luke 12:16–21), and James' picture of life as a mist that appears and vanishes (James 4:14) both stand close to Qohelet's thought.
